paragraphs: Some learning problems involve two kinds of variety at once. A single task may describe its examples through several different feature views, while several tasks may be connected through views they share. The paper calls this dual heterogeneity. Its central concern is how to use both sources of information together when learning across tasks.

The authors introduce Multi-Task Multi-View learning and a graph-based framework called GraM². The framework is designed to capture relationships among views within tasks and relationships among tasks through shared views. They also establish a connection to reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, linking the graph formulation to a mathematical setting used in kernel learning.

An iterative algorithm, IteM², provides a way to work with the framework. The paper analyzes its optimality, convergence, and computational complexity, and reports effective results on several real datasets. The contribution is a unified treatment of two forms of heterogeneity that the existing approaches discussed in the abstract address separately.
icml-2011-a-graphbased-framework-for-mul.tldr: A graph-based framework learns across related tasks and multiple feature views within a single formulation.

paragraphs: Storage problems require decisions over time under uncertainty, placing them within stochastic control. The paper introduces approximate dynamic programming for storage, abbreviated ADPS, for problems whose available decisions form continuous, convex sets. This assumption specifies the kind of decision problem the method is designed to solve.

The central computational feature is that ADPS permits mathematical programming to determine decisions in each time period, even when the state variables are large. The state describes the situation on which a decision depends. Keeping mathematical programming usable in that setting matters because a large state can make a sequential control problem difficult to handle computationally.

The authors test the method on a wind commitment problem in which commitments are made a day ahead and storage is available. This connects the proposed control method to a concrete storage application. The stated contribution is the formulation and its ability to support optimization at each decision period; the abstract reports the test application without claiming a particular numerical improvement.
icml-2011-approximate-dynamic-programmin.tldr: ADPS enables mathematical programming for sequential storage decisions with continuous, convex decision sets and large state variables.

paragraphs: A correlated equilibrium is a game-theoretic equilibrium concept that generalizes Nash equilibrium. For games represented by graphs, finding an optimal correlated equilibrium has computational complexity exponential in the graph's treewidth. The paper addresses settings where this makes exact computation infeasible but useful information about the equilibrium is still needed.

The authors study outer relaxations of the optimization problem. These provide approximations through an enlarged mathematical description of the feasible possibilities. The target quantities include players' marginal strategy probabilities and expected social utility. By focusing on these properties, the approach seeks useful equilibrium information without requiring the original exact computation.

The relaxations accommodate a variety of utility functions. Tests on simulated games and a drug-design problem indicate that the resulting approximations can be highly accurate and useful when exact methods are infeasible. This is an empirical statement about the studied applications: it supports approximation as a practical route to equilibrium properties without asserting exactness for every game.
icml-2011-approximating-correlated-equil.tldr: Outer relaxations approximate correlated-equilibrium properties and can remain highly accurate when exact computation is infeasible.

paragraphs: The most probable explanation problem asks for the most likely configuration under a probability model. The paper studies this inference problem for a family of distributions containing a particular combinatorial structure. The family permits arbitrary treewidth and factors of arbitrary size, allowing models with broad and potentially complicated interactions.

Such freedom normally presents a serious obstacle: for general models with these properties, the abstract describes the most probable explanation problem as inapproximable. The authors identify additional structure within their chosen family that changes the situation. In particular, submodularity enters indirectly and supplies the basis for algorithms with approximation guarantees.

The paper develops several such algorithms, each accompanied by a guarantee on approximation. The significance is that useful guarantees can come from the internal organization of a model even when its treewidth and factor sizes are unrestricted. The result applies to the structured family under study; arbitrary treewidth alone does not make a general probability model amenable to these methods.
icml-2011-approximation-bounds-for-infer.tldr: Embedded combinatorial structure enables guaranteed approximate inference in a model family with arbitrary treewidth and factor sizes.

paragraphs: Non-parametric kernel learning can be computationally expensive, limiting its use on large problems. This paper introduces BCDNPKL to address that scalability problem. The approach changes how the kernel-learning optimization is handled so that it avoids semidefinite programming and eigen-decomposition, two computations identified as obstacles in existing approaches.

The method rests on two findings. First, the original semidefinite programming formulation can be reduced to a much smaller problem involving a sub-kernel, called the boundary kernel. Second, this reduced learning problem can be solved efficiently through a proposed block coordinate descent technique. The reduction and solver work together: shrinking the problem creates a more manageable target for the algorithm.

The authors provide a formal proof of global convergence for BCDNPKL and evaluate it in extensive experiments against state-of-the-art algorithms. They report results supporting both scalability and effectiveness. The contribution therefore combines a smaller optimization formulation, an efficient way to solve it, and theoretical and empirical support for the resulting procedure.
icml-2011-bcdnpkl-scalable-non-parametri.tldr: BCDNPKL scales non-parametric kernel learning through a smaller boundary-kernel problem solved with block coordinate descent.

paragraphs: Bipartite ranking seeks an ordering that minimizes disagreements between pairs of examples, equivalently maximizing AUC. Working directly with those pairs creates a problem whose complexity is inherently quadratic in the number of training examples. The paper asks how much ranking quality might be sacrificed by using a loss evaluated on individual examples instead.

The answer depends on the surrogate loss. Ordinary classification error, measured by zero-one loss, can produce arbitrarily high ranking loss, so optimizing it does not provide an adequate general solution. A cost-sensitive, weighted version yields better results. The strongest developments concern margin-based losses, for which the authors derive bounds connecting individual-example optimization to ranking performance.

Those bounds cover both rank risk and rank regret, with the latter addressing the gap from the best achievable ranking risk. An experimental study investigates questions motivated by the theory. The contribution is a principled account of when simpler classification-style objectives can support ranking, together with a clear warning that ordinary classification accuracy alone is insufficient.
icml-2011-bipartite-ranking-through-mini.tldr: Margin-based losses on individual examples yield ranking guarantees, while minimizing ordinary classification error can give arbitrarily high ranking loss.

paragraphs: A classifier may perform differently across operating conditions, so a single performance number can hide useful information. For binary classification, cost-space plots display loss as those conditions change. The paper identifies an optimistic assumption in traditional cost curves: they display the best loss obtainable with the optimal decision threshold for each condition.

That presentation assumes the appropriate threshold is already known. The authors propose Brier curves, which instead put probabilistic loss on the vertical axis. This is the loss associated with the classifier's probability estimates. The resulting visualization therefore assesses those estimates across operating conditions without relying on the traditional curve's assumption of an optimally chosen threshold.

The paper also proves that the area under the proposed curve equals the Brier score, a widely used measure for probabilistic classifiers. This gives the visualization a direct connection to an established summary metric. It also provides a way to compare classifiers while inspecting how their probabilistic losses vary across the range of conditions.
icml-2011-brier-curves-a-new-cost-based-.tldr: Brier curves visualize probabilistic classifier loss across operating conditions, with area under the curve equal to the Brier score.

paragraphs: A partially observed graph distinguishes three cases: a known edge, a known absence of an edge, and an unknown relationship. The paper seeks disjoint clusters with dense observed connections inside clusters and sparse observed connections between them. Preserving the distinction between absent and unknown edges is central to the problem.

The authors formulate clustering as minimizing disagreements with the observed relationships. A known missing edge inside a cluster counts as one disagreement, as does a known present edge between clusters. They reduce this objective to recovering an unknown low-rank matrix and an unknown sparse matrix from a partially observed sum, then use convex optimization to address the recovery problem.

The analysis establishes success under assumptions about the optimal clustering and its disagreements. It also strengthens matrix-splitting results for this particular clustering setting. These conditional guarantees directly improve the treatment of correlation clustering with partial observations, connecting a graph-partitioning objective to a structured matrix-recovery formulation.
icml-2011-clustering-partially-observed-.tldr: Convex matrix recovery supports clustering partially observed graphs by minimizing disagreements with known edges and nonedges.

paragraphs: Clusterpath approaches hierarchical clustering through convex optimization. The authors propose a convex relaxation that produces a family of objective functions with a geometric interpretation. This supplies an optimization-based way to describe clustering at different settings while retaining the goal of learning hierarchical structure from data.

A central part of the method is computing a continuous regularization path: the collection of solutions obtained as regularization changes. The paper gives efficient algorithms for calculating this path and discusses the relative advantages of its parameters. Following a path makes the changing clustering structure part of the method's output, alongside the optimization formulation itself.

Experiments report state-of-the-art results comparable to spectral clustering on non-convex clusters, together with the additional benefit of a learned tree structure. Here, convexity describes the optimization formulation, while non-convexity describes the shapes of the clusters being identified. The stated findings support a method that combines competitive clustering performance in the experiments with a hierarchical description of the data.
icml-2011-clusterpath-an-algorithm-for-c.tldr: Clusterpath uses convex clustering objectives and a continuous solution path to learn clusters together with a tree structure.

paragraphs: Rule ensemble learning seeks a small collection of simple rules and suitable weights for combining them. Each rule joins basic conditions on input features. The difficulty is that all possible combinations form an exponentially large space, while interpretability and generalization favor selecting relatively few rules with relatively few conditions.

The paper applies Hierarchical Kernel Learning to explore this space efficiently. Its regularizer discourages rules containing many conditions, making the framework suitable for learning simple ensembles. Simulations show improved generalization over state-of-the-art rule ensemble methods and confirm that the approach learns simple rules.

The authors also identify an undesirable restriction: the framework selects a conjunction only when all its subsets are selected. They propose a more general convex formulation that alleviates this restriction. Their main technical contribution is an efficient active-set algorithm based on mirror descent for solving the new problem. Empirical evaluations support the usefulness of this generalized framework for rule ensemble learning.
icml-2011-efficient-rule-ensemble-learni.tldr: A generalized hierarchical-kernel formulation efficiently learns simple rule ensembles while easing an undesirable rule-selection restriction.

paragraphs: Spectral feature selection often favors features that preserve similarities among examples. The paper points out a potential problem with this strategy: a similarity matrix built from all features with equal weighting may already be unreliable when many features are noisy or irrelevant. Preserving that matrix can then encourage the selection of unsuitable features.

The authors propose assessing features by their impact on the similarity matrix. They connect this impact to changes in the graph Laplacian, which is defined from that matrix. Their Eigenvalue Sensitive Criteria, or EVSC, specifically seeks features that strongly affect the Laplacian's eigenvalues, turning the proposed notion of importance into a spectral selection criterion.

Empirical analysis finds that the method outperforms some traditional spectral feature-selection approaches. The contribution is a different basis for judging features: examining how they affect the spectral structure used to represent relationships among examples. The reported comparison supports this criterion in the studied settings without claiming that every large eigenvalue change always identifies a useful feature.
icml-2011-eigenvalue-sensitive-feature-s.tldr: EVSC selects features by their impact on graph-Laplacian eigenvalues, addressing unreliable similarities caused by noisy or irrelevant features.

paragraphs: Total variation penalties appear in statistics, signal processing, and machine learning, making their computational cost relevant to many applications. This paper studies anisotropic total variation based on the l1 norm and a related l2-norm variant. For both, it focuses on the optimization problems defining their one-dimensional proximity operators.

The authors develop Newton-type methods for these problems and report that they outperform state-of-the-art algorithms. The one-dimensional solvers also serve as building blocks for computing total variation proximity in two and higher dimensions. This connection matters because improvements to a basic optimization component can support the more difficult multidimensional computation.

The paper demonstrates computational benefits in image denoising, image deconvolution, and four fused-lasso variants. For deconvolution, the authors integrate their solvers into publicly available software, showing how the component fits into an existing application. The reported results show large speedups, and accompanying software supports those claims. The contribution centers on faster optimization routines and their use across several total-variation applications.
icml-2011-fast-newton-type-methods-for-t.tldr: Newton-type total-variation solvers accelerate one-dimensional proximity computations and support faster multidimensional applications.

paragraphs: Functional data can describe an observation through functions, and the paper considers classification when each observation contains several of them. Operator-valued kernels had attracted attention in areas including multi-task learning and functional regression, but their associated feature spaces were less well understood. The authors make that feature-space perspective central to their investigation.

They explore how the perspective can support the analysis of functional data, then extend Regularized Least Squares Classification to handle multiple functions per observation. The methodological contribution combines a way of understanding the kernel representation with an adaptation of an established classification algorithm to this richer observation format.

Experiments on a sound-recognition problem show the proposed method outperforming classical Regularized Least Squares Classification. This provides empirical support for the extension in the application studied. The broader significance is that the form of an observation can guide both the feature-space analysis and the classifier design, allowing the learning method to address several functions as components of one observation.
icml-2011-functional-regularized-least-s.tldr: An operator-valued kernel perspective extends regularized least-squares classification to observations containing multiple functions.

paragraphs: Determinantal point processes model the selection of sets when diversity is desirable. An ordinary DPP models both which items belong in a set and how large the set should be. The paper argues that this coupling can introduce unwanted content bias when an application already specifies the required number of items.

The proposed k-DPP conditions the model on selecting exactly k items. Fixing the size gives greater control and expressiveness over content and simplifies integration into applications such as search, where the number of displayed results may be predetermined. The restriction therefore aligns the model with a requirement that is already part of the task.

The authors derive efficient algorithms for normalization, sampling, and marginalization, and propose an experts-style algorithm for learning combinations of k-DPPs. These operations make the model usable for both selection and learning. In an image-search evaluation, human annotators judge k-DPP results significantly better than MMR, supporting the model's usefulness for that diversity-oriented application.
icml-2011-k-dpps-fixed-size-determinanta.tldr: k-DPPs model diverse sets of a fixed size, providing efficient inference and improved image-search results in human evaluation.

paragraphs: The paper studies a single classification task whose data appear in different feature spaces, called outlooks. Each outlook is assumed to contain both labeled and unlabeled examples. The objective is to use information from all these spaces to improve classification within each of them, despite their differing representations.

The proposed algorithm computes optimal affine mappings from the different outlooks into a target outlook. It finds these mappings by matching moments of the empirical distributions, using distributional summaries to relate the spaces. This gives a concrete way to bring information expressed in different coordinates into a common target representation.

The authors also derive a probabilistic interpretation and a sample-complexity bound describing how many examples are needed to find the mapping adequately. Extensive activity-recognition experiments show improvements in performance. Together, these contributions provide an alignment method, a theoretical account of its data requirements, and empirical evidence that sharing information across outlooks can benefit the classification task.
icml-2011-learning-from-multiple-outlook.tldr: Moment-matching affine mappings let a classifier benefit from data describing the same task in different feature spaces.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning trains several tasks jointly on the assumption that their relationships make sharing useful. This paper examines how to learn shared feature representations while also deciding which tasks should share them. The grouping of tasks becomes part of learning, so the method can discover a more selective sharing arrangement.

The authors formulate the joint choice of task groups and model parameters as a mixed integer programming problem. They use alternating minimization to solve it, updating the grouping structure and parameters through an iterative procedure. The objective decreases monotonically, and the algorithm converges to a local optimum, which specifies the scope of its optimization guarantee.

Compared with placing all tasks in one shared group, the method produces statistically significant improvements on three of the four studied datasets. The authors also report advantages over other task-grouping techniques. These findings support learning the sharing structure alongside the representation, while the three-of-four result keeps the empirical claim specific to where significant improvements were observed.
icml-2011-learning-with-whom-to-share-in.tldr: Jointly learning task groups and shared features improves over sharing across all tasks on three of four studied datasets.

paragraphs: The Dirichlet Diffusion Tree is a Bayesian nonparametric prior for modeling tree structures and hierarchies. Its practical use has been hindered in part by the computational expense of Markov chain Monte Carlo inference. The paper introduces deterministic approximate inference methods intended to make this hierarchical model more computationally accessible.

The authors develop message-passing algorithms that approximate the Bayesian model evidence for a given tree. This quantity then guides sequential tree construction and greedy search over candidate structures. The resulting trees correspond to hierarchical clusterings of the observations. The paper also presents observation models suitable for both continuous and binary data.

On a density-estimation problem, the approximate method performs very close to the computationally expensive MCMC alternative and significantly better than kernel density estimators. These results support the practical value of deterministic approximation for the tested task. The contribution connects an approximate way to score individual trees with procedures for exploring the space of hierarchical structures.
icml-2011-message-passing-algorithms-for.tldr: Deterministic message passing makes Dirichlet Diffusion Tree inference efficient while closely matching MCMC performance on a density-estimation problem.

paragraphs: This paper examines a counterintuitive possibility: a classifier can benefit from using a collection of variables dominated by irrelevant ones. The analysis concerns Boolean variables and assumes they are conditionally independent given the class. It focuses on a natural family of learning algorithms in settings where relevant variables are only slightly more informative than random guessing.

The main result identifies situations where algorithms relying predominantly on irrelevant variables have error probabilities that rapidly approach zero. In those same situations, algorithms that restrict the use of irrelevant variables retain an error bounded away from zero. This comparison challenges the expectation that aggressively limiting irrelevant variables must improve learning.

The authors also show that accurate classification can be possible with too few examples to determine confidently whether any individual variable is relevant. Taken together, the results separate successful prediction from reliable identification of useful individual features. Their force comes from the specified assumptions and learning setting; they do not establish a universal advantage for adding irrelevant variables.
icml-2011-on-the-necessity-of-irrelevant.tldr: Under the paper's assumptions, using mostly irrelevant variables can enable accurate classification even when individual relevance cannot be identified confidently.

paragraphs: The paper studies density estimation when the training sample contains contamination. It combines kernel density estimation with robust M-estimation. The starting observation is that a Gaussian-kernel density estimator can be viewed as a sample mean in its associated reproducing kernel Hilbert space, creating a route to robustifying that mean.

Using a robust loss to estimate the mean produces the robust kernel density estimator, or RKDE. A kernelized iteratively reweighted least-squares algorithm computes this estimate. The authors present a representer theorem that helps explain its robustness and give necessary and sufficient conditions for the algorithm to converge to the defining objective's global minimizer in the Gaussian kernel space.

They also characterize the estimator's influence function and provide a method for computing it, supplying a way to analyze sensitivity to contamination. Experiments on several datasets illustrate robustness. The contribution combines a robust formulation, a computational procedure, and theoretical tools for understanding both the procedure's convergence and the estimator's sensitivity.
icml-2011-on-the-robustness-of-kernel-de.tldr: Robust estimation of a kernel-space mean yields a density estimator with analyzed contamination sensitivity and conditional global-convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Online decision problems can require choosing structured objects such as trees or cuts. Many existing results assume a linear cost, allowing the cost to be expressed through separate contributions. This paper studies submodular costs, which can capture interactions that make such a separation inappropriate and the optimization problem more difficult.

The authors develop online approximation algorithms for these structured choices. Their analysis covers three strategies suited to different settings and establishes regret bounds for them. Regret measures accumulated performance relative to a benchmark, providing a way to assess decisions made over time rather than judging only an isolated optimization step.

All three strategies are described as Hannan-consistent, expressing a long-run vanishing-average-regret property in their respective settings. The paper also tightens an existing regret bound for unconstrained online submodular minimization. Its contribution is to extend the analysis of online structured decisions beyond linear costs while retaining formal performance guarantees for the proposed strategies.
icml-2011-online-submodular-minimization.tldr: Three online strategies provide regret guarantees for structured decisions with submodular costs, extending analysis beyond linear objectives.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor graphs are often used to reveal clusters, but a finite sample can also produce apparent structure that does not reflect the underlying distribution. This paper asks what these graphs reliably reveal and how to remove spurious branches from a cluster hierarchy without discarding meaningful clusters.

The first contribution analyzes particular subgraphs of a k-nearest-neighbor graph as estimators of the distribution's cluster tree. The authors establish statistical consistency, connecting the graph-based hierarchy to the underlying distribution as more data become available. This gives a theoretical basis for using those subgraphs to estimate hierarchical cluster structure.

The second contribution addresses finite samples, where pruning requires balancing aggressive removal against preservation of real structure. The paper derives a guarantee that removes all spurious cluster structures while recovering salient clusters within its analysis. This matters because an asymptotic consistency result alone does not resolve the pruning decision for a finite dataset. The authors identify their result as the first such finite-sample guarantee in clustering.
icml-2011-pruning-nearest-neighbor-clust.tldr: A statistical analysis of nearest-neighbor cluster trees gives finite-sample pruning guarantees that remove spurious structure while preserving salient clusters.

paragraphs: Some selection problems depend on information that must first be learned through queries. This paper studies that coupling through submodular set cover problems whose solution depends on an active-learning problem. The objective combines the cost of gathering information with the cost of completing the cover, so both activities are optimized together.

The authors extend this setting to tolerate a limited amount of adversarial noise. A key lemma shows that an either-or requirement involving two submodular cover constraints can be expressed as a single such constraint. Combined with existing results, this also handles arbitrary monotone circuits built from submodular cover constraints, allowing more complicated logical combinations to fit the same framework.

Certain noisy query-learning problems appear as special cases. The paper also presents a movie-recommendation website that minimizes the combined cost of discovering a user's preferences and recommending a collection of movies. This application illustrates why learning and selection belong in one objective: obtaining information is itself part of the cost of delivering recommendations.
icml-2011-simultaneous-learning-and-cove.tldr: A joint learning-and-covering framework tolerates limited adversarial noise and reduces logical combinations of submodular cover constraints to one constraint.

paragraphs: Hoeffding-based trees support prediction while learning from a continuing stream of data. One difficulty is that learning can stall when several attributes are equally useful for splitting the data. The paper addresses this delay for numerical streams, where the aim is to improve regression predictions throughout the learning process.

The proposed approach uses online option trees. These extend ordinary trees by allowing splitting options at internal nodes, accommodating alternatives when the choice of split is ambiguous. The motivation is that competing attributes need not prevent useful learning progress. Options are also associated with improvements in accuracy and stability and with reduced ambiguity.

The reported results show improved anytime performance over ordinary online regression trees, meaning better performance while learning is still underway. The method preserves an interpretable tree structure and does not significantly increase computational complexity in the reported assessment. Its contribution is a way to handle split ambiguity that improves ongoing predictive performance while retaining the practical appeal of tree-based models.
icml-2011-speeding-up-hoeffding-based-re.tldr: Online option trees improve regression learning from numerical streams by handling competing split choices without significantly increasing computational complexity.

paragraphs: A solution-path algorithm solves a sequence of related optimization problems as a parameter changes. For support vector machines, this can be useful, but maintaining strict optimality at every point along the path restricts applicability and can hurt computational efficiency. The paper investigates a path algorithm that allows controlled departures from exact optimality.

Users specify tolerances that govern how closely the solutions must satisfy optimality requirements. This creates an explicit trade-off between computational cost and solution accuracy. The method therefore treats the permitted approximation as an adjustable part of solving the sequence, with the tolerance determining how much deviation is acceptable.

The authors also show that the approximate solutions can be interpreted as solutions to perturbed versions of the original optimization problem. That interpretation supports their theoretical analysis and gives the approximation a concrete mathematical meaning. Experiments demonstrate effectiveness in efficiency and accuracy, supporting the use of controlled suboptimality to make solution-path computation more practical.
icml-2011-suboptimal-solution-path-algor.tldr: A support-vector-machine path algorithm uses user-set optimality tolerances to trade solution accuracy against computational cost.

paragraphs: Learning from demonstration asks a robot to acquire behavior from examples of correct movement. A common approach learns a mapping from states to actions that matches those examples. This paper also addresses the representation question: which dimensions of movement matter for carrying out the particular task?

The proposed method, TRIC, is inspired by inverse optimal control. It learns latent costs from demonstrated behavior and uses those costs to generate motion through a feedback controller. Learning these costs also supports discovering a task-relevant motion representation, connecting the explanation of demonstrated behavior with the way new movements are controlled.

The authors test TRIC on robot grasping, described as a challenging high-dimensional task. From a few example movements, the method learns important control dimensions and robustly approaches and grasps objects in new situations. The stated findings support its ability to imitate and generalize in this application, while making the choice of motion representation part of what is learned.
icml-2011-task-space-retrieval-using-inv.tldr: TRIC learns latent costs and task-relevant motion dimensions from demonstrations, enabling feedback-controlled grasping in new situations.
